captions.text: Recap of chapter 28: search_handbook was locked inside your Python. One folder away, it couldn't be imported.
MCP puts a tool in its own program. A request and a reply are one line of JSON each.
MCPServer turned a normal function into a real server, and by_hand.py talked to it.
Every request carries _meta now, and older servers speak only the handshake.
Today's black box: McpClient, the code that lets your agent use tools it doesn't own.
Let's open it. But first, a question your agent can't answer.
The rota is a real server, running as its own program. This agent only has search_handbook.
Ask when staff number 1042 works next, five times. Predict: what will it do?
0 of 5. It searched the handbook and found where rotas get published. It can't reach the answer.
McpClient starts the server as its own program, like by_hand.py did in chapter 28.
A thread is a second line of work. This one waits on the pipe, so your program doesn't have to.
Each line goes into a queue. When the pipe closes, None goes in, to say the server has gone.
Waiting on the queue has a timeout, so a silent server becomes an error, not a freeze.
Lines that aren't JSON go in noise. A message with another id is skipped.
connect asks server/discover. If the reply offers the new protocol, we're done.
Any other reply means try the handshake. A refusal isn't a failure here. It's the answer.
On a new server: one request to connect, then tools/list and tools/call. We hid _meta to fit.
A server's tool already has a name, a description and a schema. Only the function is missing.
So run is a stand-in. It remembers the name, and sends the arguments to the server.
The same agent and question. The only change: the server's tools join the list. Predict.
5 of 5. Agent and Toolbox didn't change, and they ran a tool in another program.
Now break it. A second program means new ways to fail. Which of these raise an exception?
A tool error is text. A wrong method is a protocol error, so it raises McpError.
A hung tool costs the whole timeout. We only stopped waiting: the tool itself is still running.
A stopped server raises at once, and a Toolbox turns that into text for the model.
So kill the server, then ask. The agent still lists get_rota. Predict: crash, or a made-up shift?
No crash. It read the error and said something was wrong. In 20 more runs, none made up a shift.
noise sets aside lines that aren't JSON. On SDK v2 it stayed empty, because v2 moves stdout.
On v1, the reply was glued onto a half-written line. 0 of 5, and no client can rescue that.
Older servers speak only the handshake. Same client, older server. Predict the first reply.
Refused with -32602. connect reads that as try the handshake, and the connection survives.
After that it's the same tools/list and tools/call. Only the opening differs.
One agent, one local tool, one new server and one older server, five runs per question.
Both servers worked, 5 of 5. The generations made no difference.
But the local search got 0 of 5. It has nothing to do with MCP. So what happened?
Eight easy handbook questions, ten runs each. Add one unrelated tool. Predict: does it matter?
77 of 80 falls to 56. Local or remote, it's the same, so this isn't MCP. It's one more tool.
Saying what each tool is for barely helped. Saying when to search reached 80 of 80, on these eight.
Now a bigger menu. Short descriptions cost about 40 tokens each, and 40 tools still mostly work.
Long descriptions held up too, while they fit: twenty tools, 3,237 tokens.
40 long tools: 12 of 60, with no error. It read 2,050 of 6,345 tokens: chapter 24's silent cut.
The same menu in a bigger window gets 55. Nothing was wrong with the tools. They didn't fit.
Did MCP itself cost anything? The same 42 questions, three runs each, local and over MCP.
Local runs twice, on purpose, to show how much two identical runs differ. Predict the gap.
110 and 109 for local, 112 for MCP. Too close to rank, so we measured no cost.
Tool text is written by someone else. This pretend server plants a line. send_note sends nothing.
Zero calls in 170 runs, even when told to obey. Read rose by 21, so the text did arrive.
But that score only counts tool calls. Read what it said to the user.
100 of 100 passed the planted request on, as if it came from Quillon. That's not safety. Chapter 31.
McpClient is plain Python, so you can read it, and this course doesn't teach async.
Production code would use the official SDK's client, which is async, and handles far more.
Your turn. Open exercises.py and complete the five TODOs.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.

points: A server's tool is a Tool
Run your eval when tools change

captions.text: Your agent can use tools it doesn't own, and MCP itself cost nothing we could measure.
But each tool changes your prompt, and tools have to fit in the window. Run your eval again.
Those counts come from one 7B model on one Mac. Test yours.
